title: Whole-body clearing of beetles by successive treatment of hydrogen peroxide and CUBIC reagents
author: Monto Kuroda

materials: Nitrilotriethanol (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Co. cat. no. 145-05605) 69 Sucrose (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Co. cat. no. 196-00015) 70 71 METHODS and RESULTS 72 The method we developed for whole-body clearing of large beetles consisted of three 73 steps: I. Fixation, II. Bleaching of exoskeleton by hydrogen peroxide and III. Whole-body 74 clearing by the advanced CUBIC. 75 Step I. Fixation. We rehydrated the dry specimen of Dorcus titanus typhon, Trypoxylus 76 dichotomus, and Rhomborrhina japonica in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) (pH 7.4). 77 We prepared alcoholic formalin by diluting 10% formaldehyde neutral buffer solution 78 with three volumes of ethanol (Koga et al, 2009). We fixed them with alcoholic formalin 79 at 37℃ for a week, and washed them with PBS three times. 80 Step II. Bleaching of exoskeleton by hydrogen peroxide. We incubated the fixed 81 samples with 6% H2O2/ethanol (30% H2O2 diluted with four volumes of ethanol) at 37 /i1 82 for 14 weeks (Figure 2) ( Koga et al , 2009) , replacing the 6% H 2O2/ethanol twice per 83 week. Note that do not fix the cap tightly because bubbles are formed. After the bleaching, 84 we washed the bleached samples with PBS three times. 85 Step III． Whole-body clearing by the advanced CUBIC. We performed the whole-body 86 clearing according to the advanced CUBIC (Susaki et al, 2015). We prepared reagent 1, 87 containing 25%(w/w) Urea, 25%(w/w) Quadrol, and 15%(w/w) Triton X-100. We 88 incubated the bleached samples with 1/2 reagent 1 (reagent 1 diluted with an equal 89 volume of water) at 37 /i1 for 2 days. We then replaced 1/2 reagent 1 to reagent 1. We 90 exchanged reagent 1 twice per week, and incubated for 5 weeks (Figure 3). 91 We then prepared reagent 2, containing 25%(w/w) Urea, 50%(w/w) Sucrose, 10%(w/w) 92 nitrilotriethanol. We incubated the reagent 1-treated samples with 1/2 reagent 2 (reagent 2 93 diluted with an equal volume of PBS) at 37℃ for 1 day. We then replaced 1/2 reagent 2 to 94 reagent 2. We exchanged reagent 2 every week, and incubated for 2 weeks (Figure 4). 95 Washing the reagent 2-treated samples with PBS decreased the transparency, so we kept 96 the final samples in the reagent 2. 97 We compared our method with other methods (Table, Figure 5). Only our method, but 98 not other methods, succeeded in making large beetles transparent. The differences 99 between our methods and others are the combination of hydrogen peroxide, which 100 bleaches exoskeletons, and CUBIC, which clears both bleached exoskeletons and internal 101 tissues, with much longer incubation time. The combination of hydrogen peroxide and 102 CUBIC in this study was the same as the method used by Konno and Okazaki, however, 103

our method used a longer incubation time with both hydrogen peroxide and CUBIC, 104 which enabled the whole-body clearing of the beetles. 105 106 DISCUSSION 107 In this study, we developed a method of whole-body clearing of large beetles which 108 combined bleaching exoskeletons using hydrogen peroxide with whole-body clearing 109 using CUBIC. During the bleaching process, when ethanol was used as a solvent (Koga 110 et al , 2009), the internal tissue was sufficiently fixed during the whole procedure, but 111 when water was used as a solvent (Konno and Okazaki, 2018), the internal tissue was not 112 sufficiently fixed (data not shown). Therefore, ethanol should be used as the solvent 113 during bleaching with hydrogen peroxide. Furthermore, while our study bleached the 114 large beetles for 14 weeks, this did not completely bleach them. A longer bleaching 115 duration may be required to completely bleach exoskeletons. The whole-body clearing by 116 CUBIC required about 3 months, which is longer than required for clearing mouse tissues 117 (about 2 weeks) (Susaki et al, 2015). The use of the latest CUBIC reagents (Tainaka et al, 118 2018) may shorten this long-term treatment by the current protocol. We did not perform 119 nuclear staining, and did not visualize the internal tissues. It remains unclear whether the 120 internal tissues are correctly fixed. 121 122 ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 123 We thank Drs. steps.instruction: Fix the specimens using Formalin/Ethanol for 1 week.

steps.title: Bleach the specimens
steps.instruction: Incubate the samples in 6% H2O2/ethanol for 14 weeks.

steps.title: Clear the specimens using CUBIC
steps.instruction: Perform whole-body clearing using CUBIC reagents over a total of 7 weeks.

description: Abstract 18 Internal tissues of multicellular organisms cannot directly be seen because they contain 19 pigments. For this reason, whole-body clearing methods have been developed and applied 20 to mammals such as mice. Insects such as beetles, however, cannot be cleared by the 21 mammalian method because of pigments such as melanin in their exoskeletons. In this 22 study, we tried to develop a whole-body clearing method for large beetles. We first 23 bleached the exoskeleton using a hydrogen peroxide treatment, and applied the the 24 advanced Clear, Unobstructed Brain/Body Imaging Cocktails and Computational analysis 25 (CUBIC) reagents to make the internal tissues transparent. The combined method of 26 hydrogen peroxide and the advanced CUBIC allowed us to successfully perform 27 whole-body clearing of the large beetles. 28 29 Key words: Whole-body clearing, hydrogen peroxide, CUBIC, Trypoxylus dichotomus, 30 Rhomborrhina japonica, Dorcus titanus typhon 31 32 INTRODUCTION 33 Mammalian tissues are opaque because they contain pigments that absorb visible light, 34 such as hemoglobin, and myoglobin; substances that scatter light, such as lipids; and 35 autofluorescent substances that interfere with the visualization of fluorescently labeled 36 substances such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate hydrogen and collagen. 37 Recently, whole-body clearing methods have been developed to make mammalian tissues 38 transparent (Tainaka et al , 2016). However, these methods do not make insects 39 transparent because of pigments such as melanin in their exoskeletons (Noh et al, 2016). 40 Hydrogen peroxide has been used to bleach insect exoskeletons and make them 41 transparent (Koga et al , 2009).
